f.p: Peter the Great Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (Kunstkamera), Russian Academy of Sciences
f.t: Researchers at Russia's Kunstkamera museum published a 2018 study on the mobile dwellings of Chukchi reindeer herders, covering both traditions and innovations.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Carving bone and walrus ivory and embroidering with reindeer hair are long-standing Chukchi arts, practised alongside reindeer herding and hunting.

f.p: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)
f.t: Chukchi have used pictographs since ancient times, and their oldest known documents are inscribed walrus tusks.

n.l: Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, northern Kamchatka Krai and the Nizhnekolymsky District of Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: During an August 2026 folk culture expedition to Khatanga, the Dolgan dried-fish dish kerdiileek was added to the list of Taimyr's intangible cultural heritage.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Dolgan is a Turkic language, close to Sakha (Yakut), from which it separated through isolated development.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: The Dolgan formed as a people in the north of the Yenisei region between the 17th and 19th centuries and took final shape in the early 20th century.

n.l: Taimyr Peninsula in Krasnoyarsk Krai (Taimyr Dolgan-Nenets District) and the Anabar District and city of Yakutsk in Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: The 2002 census counted 11,657 Even living in the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia).

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Sharing holds a valued place in Even life: the custom of dividing a catch, called nimat, has traditionally played an important role.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: The Even language belongs to the Tungusic (Manchu-Tungus) branch and is close to Evenki. Even self-names include Even (local) and Orochel (reindeer people).

n.l: Northeastern Siberia: Sakha (Yakutia), Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka, Chukotka and Khabarovsk Krai, Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Evenki communities live across Russia, with the largest in Sakha (Yakutia), and Evenki also live in China and Mongolia.

f.p: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)
f.t: Evenki homelands span a huge part of the Siberian taiga, from the Ob River in the west to the Sea of Okhotsk in the east.

n.l: Siberian taiga from the Ob River to the Sea of Okhotsk, with the largest group in Sakha (Yakutia), also Krasnoyarsk and Khabarovsk krais, Buryatia, Amur, Irkutsk and Zabaykalsky regions of Russia, and in China and Mongolia

f.p: Lex, Danmarks Nationalleksikon
f.t: The Inughuit have their own language, or dialect, and a hunting culture that is distinctive in several ways.

f.p: Peary-MacMillan Arctic Museum, Bowdoin College
f.t: Arctic explorers relied on Inughuit skill and knowledge of the far north to succeed, and Inughuit elders later shared their knowledge to help a US museum document that history.

f.p: Lex, Danmarks Nationalleksikon
f.t: Hunting is still a significant part of the livelihood of several families in Qaanaaq, Greenland's youngest and northernmost town.

n.l: Avanersuaq (the Thule region) in northwest Greenland, centred on the town of Qaanaaq

f.p: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)
f.t: The self-name Itelmen means an inhabitant of dry land, a human being.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Fishing, above all for salmon, is the traditional Itelmen livelihood on Kamchatka.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Western Itelmen is the Itelmen language that has been kept to the present day.

n.l: Tigilsky District on the west coast of Kamchatka Krai, with smaller groups in Chukotka and Magadan Oblast, Russia

f.p: Prime Minister's Office of Denmark (Statsministeriet)
f.t: Under the Self-Government Act, in force since 21 June 2009, the people of Greenland are recognised as a people with the right to self-determination under international law.

f.p: Prime Minister's Office of Denmark (Statsministeriet)
f.t: The Self-Government Act recognises Greenlandic (Kalaallisut) as the official language of Greenland.

f.p: Oqaasileriffik (Language Secretariat of Greenland)
f.t: Standard Greenlandic grew out of central West Greenland speech and is the written language every Greenlander shares, while anyone may speak in their own dialect.

n.l: Kalaallit Nunaat (Greenland), which has self-government within the Kingdom of Denmark

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: A Cyrillic writing system that Ket speakers actually use came into being in the late 1980s.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Ket is the only living language of the Yeniseian language family.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Hunting and fishing are at the heart of Ket tradition; fish, moose, deer and wild birds have long sustained Ket life on the Yenisei.

n.l: Yenisei River basin, mainly Turukhansky District of Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia

f.p: Khanty Mansi Mir (joint editorial office of the Khanty Yasang and Luima Seripos newspapers)
f.t: The first newspaper in the Khanty language in the okrug came out on 1 November 1957. Known today as Khanty Yasang, it is still made by a joint Khanty and Mansi newsroom.

f.p: Arctic Anthropology blog, Arctic Centre, University of Lapland
f.t: For many Khanty families, fishing and reindeer herding are closely intertwined, and family fishing hamlets on rivers like the Synia still carry clan surnames.

f.p: Fenno-Ugria Foundation
f.t: Khanty belongs to the Ugric group of the Finno-Ugric languages, together with Mansi and Hungarian.

n.l: River valleys of the Ob basin in western Siberia: Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug (Yugra), Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Tomsk Oblast, Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: In 2000, a Russian government decree gave the Koryak the status of an Indigenous small-numbered people.

f.p: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)
f.t: Koryaks call themselves by two names: nomadic reindeer-herding groups use Chavchu, meaning reindeer rearers, and settled groups use Nymylan, meaning settlers.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Reindeer herding was the main way of life for nomadic Koryaks, while settled Koryaks mostly fished and hunted sea mammals.

n.l: Mainly the north of Kamchatka Krai, Russian Far East

f.p: Khanty Mansi Mir (joint editorial office of the Khanty Yasang and Luima Seripos newspapers)
f.t: Luima Seripos, a newspaper in the Mansi language, first came out on 11 February 1989 and is still produced today in a joint newsroom with the Khanty paper.

f.p: Fenno-Ugria Foundation
f.t: Mansi rapper Yevgeny Anyamov, known as Bizzo, records his songs in Mansi and opened his own studio in his hometown of Ivdel to share his people's culture with youth.

f.p: Fenno-Ugria Foundation
f.t: Russia's 2010 census counted 12,269 Mansi, up from 11,432 in 2002.

n.l: Ob and Irtysh basin in western Siberia, mainly Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug (Yugra), with small groups in Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Nanai communities also live in China, where about 4,600 Nanai were counted in 2000.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Clothing sewn from fish skin is a hallmark of traditional Nanai craft, rooted in a life of fishing on the Amur River.

f.p: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)
f.t: Nanai decorative art is known for its richly developed ornament.

n.l: Lower Amur River valley in Khabarovsk Krai and Primorsky Krai, Russia, and the Sungari River area of northeast China

f.p: Fenno-Ugria Foundation
f.t: In Yamal, a regional grant helps young Nenets, Khanty and other Indigenous nomadic families with three or more children equip a chum shelter. By 2024, 268 families had received it.

f.p: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)
f.t: Nenets belongs to the Samoyedic branch of the Uralic languages and has two main dialects, Tundra and Forest.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Nenets reindeer herders are regarded today as the most mobile nomads in the world, with large-herd reindeer herding at the heart of the tundra economy.

n.l: Tundra and forest-tundra from the Kola Peninsula to the Yenisei River, including the Nenets and Yamal-Nenets autonomous okrugs and Taimyr, Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: In August 2026, a state folk culture expedition in Taimyr met a knowledge keeper of Vadeyev Nganasan culture, who showed traditional dishes and how Nganasan cuisine differs from Dolgan.

f.p: Fenno-Ugria Foundation
f.t: The Nganasan are the northernmost Indigenous people of Eurasia, living on the Taimyr Peninsula near the Arctic Ocean.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Nganasan belongs to the Samoyedic branch of the Uralic-Yukaghir language family.

n.l: Southern and central Taimyr Peninsula, Krasnoyarsk Krai, including the villages of Ust-Avam, Volochanka and Novaya and the towns of Dudinka and Norilsk, Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Nivkh life was built on fishing and hunting, including sea mammals taken with spears or with nets woven from leather straps.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: The Nivkh speak a language isolate, probably one of the oldest languages of Eurasia. Its links to other languages have not been established.

n.l: Lower Amur River in Khabarovsk Krai and Sakhalin Island, Russia

f.p: Sámediggi (Sámi Parliament of Finland)
f.t: About 10,000 Sámi live in Finland, where three Sámi languages are spoken: Northern Sámi, Inari Sámi and Skolt Sámi.

f.p: Sámediggi (Sámi Parliament of Norway)
f.t: Norway's Sámi Parliament is elected by and among the Sámi. First opened in Karasjok in 1989, it now has 39 representatives from seven constituencies.

f.p: Saami Council (Sámiráđđi)
f.t: February 6 is Sámi National Day, celebrated all over Sápmi. The Sámi flag and anthem were both adopted at the Saami Conference held in Åre, Sweden, in 1986.

n.l: Sápmi, across northern Norway, Sweden and Finland and the Kola Peninsula of Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Since a 2000 government decree, Russia has listed the Selkup as an Indigenous small-numbered people.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Selkup belongs to the Samoyedic group of the Uralic language family.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Selkup self-names differ by river: sölkup or shölkup on the Taz and Turukhan, and chumylkup on the Vasyugan, Parabel and Tym.

n.l: Between the middle Ob and Yenisei rivers: the Taz River area of Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and the Narym area of Tomsk Oblast, Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: The Udehe language belongs to the Amur group of the Tungusic (Manchu-Tungus) languages.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: In the Udehe yearly cycle, taiga hunting was combined with fishing and gathering.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Most Udehe today live in villages on the Khor and Bikin rivers in Russia's Far East.

n.l: Villages on the Khor and Bikin rivers in Khabarovsk Krai and Primorsky Krai, and towns of both regions, Russia

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: A Cyrillic-based writing system for Yukaghir was developed in the 1970s.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Using dogs for transport is a widespread Yukaghir tradition, and the people were originally settled hunters and fishers.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Today the Yukaghir speak two languages: Northern (Tundra) Yukaghir and Southern (Kolyma) Yukaghir.

n.l: Kolyma River basin in the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia) and Magadan Oblast, Russia

f.p: Inuit Circumpolar Council Canada
f.t: Inuit from Chukotka became part of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 1992, a goal that was in ICC's vision from the very beginning.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Yupik hunters are regarded as originators of traditional whaling in the region, hunting walrus, seal and whale with harpoons.

f.p: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)
f.t: Carving walrus ivory and whale baleen is a highly developed Yupik craft in Chukotka.

n.l: Settlements on the eastern coast of the Chukchi Peninsula, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, Russia, across the Bering Strait from Alaska
